stem: A nurse begins discharge planning early for a client hospitalized with acute ischemic stroke. Which plan best reflects current stroke-care guidance?

options.A: Use an individualized, evolving plan based on patient and family needs that addresses postacute rehabilitation and services, medication and secondary-prevention education, follow-up, safety and self-management needs, and caregiver readiness before transition.
options.B: Use the same discharge template for every stroke survivor because functional deficits, home environment, caregiver support, and rehabilitation needs do not change the transition plan.
options.C: Wait until the day of discharge to begin planning because early needs assessment does not affect selection of postacute services or caregiver preparation.
options.D: Focus only on the discharge date and medication list because rehabilitation placement, recurrent-stroke education, caregiver training, and follow-up are handled after the client leaves the hospital.

rationale: A is correct. A 2026 AHA scientific statement on nursing stroke care states that discharge planning should begin early, remain dynamic, and be guided by patient and family needs assessments; predischarge rehabilitation assessment is important for selecting the appropriate postacute setting and services. Current AHA nursing guidance also emphasizes education about lifestyle changes, medication adherence, recurrent-stroke symptom recognition, self-management and secondary prevention, and preparation of caregivers before discharge. B, C, and D fail to individualize the transition or defer essential planning until too late.
educational_objective: Plan stroke discharge as an early, dynamic, individualized transition process that integrates rehabilitation/service needs, medications and secondary prevention, follow-up and safety/self-management planning, and caregiver education/readiness.
source_document_title: Targeted Nursing Interventions for Improving Stroke Care and Outcomes in the Rural Setting; Care of the Patient With Acute Ischemic Stroke (Posthyperacute and Prehospital Discharge)
source_version_date: Rural stroke nursing scientific statement published January 2026; posthyperacute/discharge scientific statement published 2021 and cited as associated guidance in the 2026 AIS guideline; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: 2026 Targeted Nursing Interventions — Posthyperacute and Discharge: nurses educate about lifestyle changes, medication adherence, and early recurrent-stroke symptom recognition; discharge planning should begin early and remain dynamic based on patient/family needs; predischarge rehabilitation assessments help determine appropriate postacute setting and services. 2021 Posthyperacute/Predischarge statement and AHA commentary: discharge planning includes self-management, secondary stroke prevention, and caregiver education/readiness before discharge. 2026 AIS Guideline Section 5.7 supports multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation evaluation for appropriate postacute rehabilitation level.
source_claim_supported: Stroke discharge planning should begin early, remain individualized and dynamic, incorporate rehabilitation/postacute service selection and secondary-prevention/self-management education, and prepare patients and caregivers for the transition rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all last-day process.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: coordinate transitions of care, assess needs for referrals/resources, provide discharge planning and education, and collaborate with clients, caregivers, and the interdisciplinary team.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized stroke discharge and transition planning
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw generic discharge list into a current, dynamic transition-of-care item using the January 2026 AHA rural stroke nursing statement plus the AHA posthyperacute/discharge guidance referenced by the 2026 AIS guideline. The final item avoids implying that one fixed set of services is required for every stroke survivor and emphasizes patient/family needs and caregiver readiness.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against the January 2026 AHA rural stroke nursing scientific statement, the AHA posthyperacute/predischarge nursing statement, and the 2026 AIS rehabilitation guidance.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A integrates early dynamic planning, rehabilitation/service assessment, secondary prevention, follow-up and caregiver preparation. B falsely standardizes every transition. C delays needs assessment. D omits essential predischarge coordination and education.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; individualized early multidisciplinary transition planning.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; post-stroke needs vary substantially among patients and families.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; current guidance explicitly supports early dynamic planning.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; rehabilitation, education, caregiver readiness and follow-up must be addressed before transition.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A does not mandate identical services or a specific discharge destination; it requires assessment-driven planning, leaving it uniquely correct.
audit_findings.cueing: All options describe competing discharge-planning models.
audit_findings.blueprint: Transitions, referrals, education and caregiver coordination fit Management of Care.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked current 2026 discharge wording, caregiver-readiness evidence, rehabilitation placement, secondary-prevention education and rural-resource caveats. The final answer remains individualized and avoids unsupported fixed timelines or service requirements. No second defensible answer remained.
